features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: New Spain
features.source: From the fall of Tenochtitlan: the central Mexican domain Spain took over from the Triple Alliance, about 180,000 km² against Cliopatria's 216,000 for its 1521 slice.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: New Spain
features.source: West to Michoacán and Colima and south into Oaxaca, about 410,000 km²; Cliopatria has 457,000 inside modern Mexico by 1526.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: New Spain
features.source: The viceroyalty established in 1535, with the silver country north of the valley; Cliopatria has 750,000 km² by 1534 against the 570,000 drawn here, which stays with the settled ground rather than the claim.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: New Spain
features.source: The conquest of Yucatán closed the last Mayan city-states in 1546, which is why the peninsula and Chiapas join here; about 900,000 km², matching Cliopatria's 895,000 for 1547.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: New Spain
features.source: Nueva Vizcaya and the northern mining frontier; Cliopatria's mainland jumps to 1.26 million km² in 1595 and holds near there for most of the century.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: New Spain
features.source: Sonora, Coahuila and Nuevo León; about 1.53 million km² against Cliopatria's 1.56 million for 1687.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: New Spain
features.source: By 1700 New Spain holds effectively all of modern Mexico — Cliopatria puts it at 1.97 million km² — so the modern-boundary parts take over from the drawn frontier here.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: New Spain
features.source: The province of Tejas, garrisoned from 1716 and settled at San Antonio in 1718, drawn with the modern Texas extent.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: New Spain
features.source: Portolá and Serra occupied Alta California in 1769, which is when the Pacific northwest of New Spain becomes more than a claim.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: New Mexico (Spain)
features.source: Oñate's colony on the upper Rio Grande, drawn separately because the part it sits in — the later Mexican Cession — does not become Spanish in fact until Alta California in 1769. It ends here at the Pueblo Revolt, which drove the Spanish out of the province entirely.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: New Mexico (Spain)
features.source: Vargas's reconquest returned the province to Spain twelve years after the revolt; the resettlement that made it hold followed in December 1693.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: Guatemala (Spain)
features.source: Alvarado's conquest of the Guatemalan highlands. It stops short of the Petén, which the Itza Mayans held until 1697, and so is drawn as Guatemala without its northern lowlands.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: Guatemala (Spain)
features.source: San Salvador, Honduras and Nicaragua, conquered in the same campaigns of 1524-25 and drawn with their modern extents.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: Costa Rica (Spain)
features.source: Cartago founded in 1563, the first lasting Spanish settlement in Costa Rica.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: Guatemala (Spain)
features.source: The Captaincy General of Guatemala, governed from Antigua and then Guatemala City; the Petén joins it once the Itza were subdued.

features.label: Louisiana (Spain)
features.source: Ceded by France in 1762 and handed back at San Ildefonso in 1800.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: Florida (Spain)
features.source: St. Augustine, founded in 1565, was the first durable Spanish settlement in Florida; the claims from Ponce de León's 1513 landing onward are not drawn. Held until Britain acquired it at the Treaty of Paris.

features.label: Florida (Spain)
features.source: Recovered from Britain in 1783 and given up to the United States under Adams-Onis.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: Venezuela (Spain)
features.source: Nueva Toledo, planted at Cumaná in 1521, was destroyed in the 1522 uprising; the durable fort town of Nueva Córdoba followed in 1523. It is shown as a small eastern foothold, not as possession of the future Venezuela.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: Venezuela (Spain)
features.source: Coro, founded in 1527, added the first lasting western Spanish settlement; the two distant footholds are kept separate.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: Venezuela (Spain)
features.source: El Tocuyo (1545) and Barquisimeto (1552) grew the Coro foothold into a western settlement zone, while Cumaná remained a separate eastern outpost.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: Venezuela (Spain)
features.source: Valencia, founded in 1555, extended the connected western settlement belt eastward; Cumaná remains separate.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: Venezuela (Spain)
features.source: Caracas was founded in 1567, joining the central coast to the older western settlements in one continuous belt; Cumaná stays as the separate eastern outpost. The province is still not represented by Venezuela's full modern outline.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: Venezuela (Spain)
features.source: Maracaibo, refounded in 1574, is drawn continuous with the Coro–Barquisimeto belt across the lake approaches rather than as an isolated port; only Cumaná remains a separate eastern outpost.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: Venezuela (Spain)
features.source: Trujillo, Carora, Barinas and Guanare filled the interior in the late sixteenth century, so from 1600 the province is drawn as one continuous core from Maracaibo to Cumaná. The Orinoco basin, Guiana and the southern interior stay outside this effective-settlement extent.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: Panama (Spain)
features.source: Panamá founded on the Pacific in 1519, the isthmus crossing that everything Spanish in the Pacific went through; Cliopatria's earliest American slice, in 1516, is this coast and Darién.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: Santa Marta (Spain)
features.source: Santa Marta, founded in 1525, is the first durable Spanish foothold in what is now Colombia; it is not yet a claim to the whole country.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: Caribbean New Granada (Spain)
features.source: Cartagena, founded in 1533, added a second Caribbean settlement to Santa Marta; Spanish rule is still represented as two coastal centres.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: New Granada (Spain)
features.source: Cali, founded in 1536, added the first major inland settlement in the Cauca valley to the two Caribbean ports.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: New Granada (Spain)
features.source: Popayán and Pasto, founded in 1537 along Belalcázar's road north, are drawn as one continuous Cauca-and-Andes corridor with Cali rather than as isolated towns.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: New Granada (Spain)
features.source: The conquest of the Bogotá highlands in 1538 is drawn with the Magdalena river corridor that carried it — Mompox was planted on the river in 1537 — running continuously from the Caribbean ports to Santafé.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: New Granada (Spain)
features.source: Tunja and Vélez, founded in 1539, carried the highland settlement northeast, continuous with Santafé and the river corridor.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: New Granada (Spain)
features.source: Antioquia, founded in 1541, is drawn continuous with the Cauca valley corridor that reached and supplied it.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: New Granada (Spain)
features.source: Pamplona was founded and the Audiencia of Santafé decreed in 1549; from here the corridors are drawn knit into one broad Caribbean-and-Andean core. The Amazon, the Orinoco plains and much of the Pacific lowlands stay outside this effective-settlement extent.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: Quito (Spain)
features.source: Quito and Riobamba, founded in 1534 along the conquest road, are drawn as one continuous inter-Andean strip; Portoviejo of 1535 is a separate coastal centre.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: Quito (Spain)
features.source: Guayaquil, traditionally dated to its 1538 founding by Orellana, is drawn joined to the highland strip along the Babahoyo route rather than as an island of settlement.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: Quito (Spain)
features.source: Loja, settled at its lasting site in 1548, and Zamora, founded from it in 1549, extended the network south and east of the early highland and coastal centres.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: Quito (Spain)
features.source: Cuenca, founded in 1557, closed the last gap in the inter-Andean chain, so the coastal and highland settlements are drawn as one continuous core; Zamora hangs on beyond it in the eastern lowlands.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: Quito (Spain)
features.source: The Jívaro uprising of 1599 destroyed the eastern lowland towns, leaving the connected core; the sparsely settled Amazonian slope stays outside until independence.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: Paraguay (Spain)
features.source: Asunción, founded in 1537, was the base for everything Spanish on the upper Plata, and the Guaraní towns around it — Ita, Yaguarón and Tobatí in 1539 — are drawn with it as one district rather than as separate points.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: Paraguay (Spain)
features.source: The Jesuit reductions begun at San Ignacio Guazú in 1609 and Itapúa in 1615 put a second settled zone on the Paraná, still separate from the Asunción district.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: Paraguay (Spain)
features.source: The governorate of Paraguay was split from Río de la Plata in 1617, and the towns and reductions between Asunción and the Paraná — Villarrica at its lasting site from 1682, Curuguaty in 1715 — knit into one continuous eastern core. The Chaco west of the Paraguay river stays outside it.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: Paraguay (Spain)
features.source: Villa Real de la Concepción, founded in 1773, carried settlement up the river to the northern frontier and completed the Región Oriental. The Gran Chaco, about three-fifths of modern Paraguay, is left out for the whole colonial period: it stayed in Guaycurú and Payaguá hands past independence and was not settled until the twentieth century.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: Tucumán (Spain)
features.source: Santiago del Estero, founded in 1553, was the first Spanish town in Argentina to last; the Buenos Aires of 1536 had been abandoned. San Miguel de Tucumán followed in 1565 and is drawn continuous with it, not as a second point.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: Tucumán (Spain)
features.source: Córdoba and Santa Fe, both founded in 1573, opened the road from the Tucumán towns down to the Paraná and are drawn as one continuous band with them.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: Río de la Plata (Spain)
features.source: Garay refounded Buenos Aires in 1580, giving the province its Atlantic port, and Salta (1582), Corrientes (1588), La Rioja (1591) and Jujuy (1593) filled in behind it. The settled ground runs up the Paraná and along the Córdoba road, not across the Chaco between them.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: Río de la Plata (Spain)
features.source: Río de la Plata was split from Paraguay as its own governorate in 1617, and the Tucumán towns, the Córdoba road and the Litoral had knit into one core. The southern edge is the frontier the Spanish actually held: the Pampas beyond the Salado, Patagonia and the deep Chaco stayed in Mapuche, Tehuelche and Guaycurú hands.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: Río de la Plata (Spain)
features.source: The Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata was created in 1776 and Cuyo passed to it from Chile, joining Mendoza and San Juan to Córdoba in one extent. Carmen de Patagones, founded on the Río Negro in 1779, is the one Spanish foothold in Patagonia and is drawn alone in it.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: Río de la Plata (Spain)
features.source: Soriano on the Río Negro, the first lasting settlement in the Banda Oriental; represented with Uruguay's modern extent until Portuguese occupation.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: Chile (Spain)
features.source: Valdivia founded Santiago in 1541 and La Serena in 1544; the central valley between them is drawn as one strip rather than two towns. The Atacama north of it stayed a desert march under Charcas, not Chile.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: Chile (Spain)
features.source: Concepción (1550), Valdivia, Villarrica and Imperial (1552), Angol (1553) and Osorno (1558) carried Spanish settlement through Araucanía to the southern lakes, the deepest it ever reached on the mainland.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: Chile (Spain)
features.source: Mendoza (1561), San Juan (1562) and later San Luis were founded across the Andes and governed from Santiago, so Cuyo is drawn Chilean; Castro on Chiloé followed in 1567, reached by sea and kept separate.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: Chile (Spain)
features.source: The Mapuche victory at Curalaba in December 1598 was followed by the destruction of every Spanish city south of the Bío-Bío by 1604. Spain fell back to the river and never recovered the ground; Chiloé was left cut off behind the frontier.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: Chile (Spain)
features.source: Valdivia was refounded in 1645 as a walled garrison supplied by sea, an enclave rather than a return to Araucanía. The parliament of Quillín had recognised the Bío-Bío as the frontier in 1641, and it held until the republic's campaigns of 1861-83.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: Chile (Spain)
features.source: Cuyo was detached from Chile in 1776 for the new Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata. Osorno was refounded in 1796 but the Bío-Bío line was still the limit at independence; Chiloé held out for Spain until January 1826.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: Peru (Spain)
features.source: Piura was founded in 1532 and Atahualpa taken at Cajamarca that November, but the Inca state is drawn holding the country until 1534. From the Spanish refounding of Cusco and Jauja that year the conquest is drawn as one continuous band down the highland road, not as separate towns. It bends south of the Apurímac to leave the neo-Inca Vilcabamba outside.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: Peru (Spain)
features.source: Lima, founded in January 1535 as the seat of government, joined the coast to the sierra road; Trujillo followed the same year. Manco Inca's rising besieged both Lima and Cusco in 1536 without breaking the hold.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: Peru (Spain)
features.source: Chachapoyas (1538), Huamanga and Huánuco (1539) and Arequipa (1540) closed the gaps, so from 1540 the coast and sierra are drawn as one core running the length of the country. The viceroyalty was created in 1542 and the Audiencia of Lima opened in 1544; the Amazon selva stays outside effective settlement, and Vilcabamba is still cut out of it.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: Peru (Spain)
features.source: Tupac Amaru was taken at Vilcabamba in 1572 and Toledo's reforms fixed Spanish rule on the whole country, so the modern extent takes over from the drawn core here. The selva is included on the viceroyalty's jurisdiction rather than on settlement, which reached it only with the Maynas missions from 1638.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: Upper Peru (Spain)
features.source: La Plata, the Charcas town later called Sucre, was founded in 1538 as the first durable Spanish seat in Upper Peru.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: Upper Peru (Spain)
features.source: Potosí, founded on the silver mountain in 1545, is drawn continuous with La Plata rather than as an isolated camp; the two were a single administrative and supply district from the start.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: Upper Peru (Spain)
features.source: La Paz, founded in 1548 on the road carrying Potosí's silver north to Cusco, made the altiplano one continuous settled axis from Titicaca to the mines.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: Upper Peru (Spain)
features.source: The Audiencia of Charcas was erected in 1559 over the whole of Upper Peru, and Santa Cruz (1561), Cochabamba (1571) and Tarija (1574) filled in behind it. The Beni and Chiquitos lowlands are drawn on that jurisdiction rather than on settlement, which reached them only with the Jesuit missions of the 1680s and 1690s; the Chaco was never effectively held.

features.label: Falkland Islands (Spain)
features.source: Spain administered Puerto Soledad after France's withdrawal until the settlement was evacuated during the independence wars.

features.name: Crown of Castile
features.label: Baracoa (Crown of Castile)
features.source: Diego Velázquez's 1511 expedition established Baracoa, Cuba's first Spanish settlement. Columbus's 1492 landing is not treated as occupation, and this first foothold is not yet drawn as the whole island.

features.name: Crown of Castile
features.label: Eastern Cuba (Crown of Castile)
features.source: The colony spread west from Baracoa with Bayamo in 1513 while Narváez's columns swept the rest of the island; durable settlement was still eastern.

features.name: Crown of Castile
features.label: Cuba (Crown of Castile)
features.source: The villas of 1514 — Trinidad, Sancti Spíritus, Puerto Príncipe and Havana — spanned the conquered island, with Santiago de Cuba following in 1515, so Cuba is drawn whole from here.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: Cuba (Spain)
features.source: Passed to the Spanish Empire at the 1516 succession; lost to the United States in the Treaty of Paris.

features.name: Crown of Castile
features.label: Puerto Rico (Crown of Castile)
features.source: Juan Ponce de León established Caparra, the first permanent Spanish settlement, in 1508. Columbus's 1493 landing is not treated as occupation.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: Puerto Rico (Spain)
features.source: Ceded to the United States in the Treaty of Paris.

features.name: Crown of Castile
features.label: La Isabela (Crown of Castile)
features.source: La Isabela, founded in January 1494 on Hispaniola's north coast, was Spain's first durable settlement in the Americas; it is shown as a small colonial foothold rather than the future Dominican Republic.

features.name: Crown of Castile
features.label: Santo Domingo (Crown of Castile)
features.source: The new south-coast settlement of Santo Domingo was founded in 1496 and became the colonial base while Spanish conquest of the rest of Hispaniola continued.

features.name: Crown of Castile
features.label: Santo Domingo (Crown of Castile)
features.source: After the conquest of the eastern end of Hispaniola, the Spanish colony is drawn across the island rather than leaving the future Haitian west empty.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: Santo Domingo (Spain)
features.source: Spanish Santo Domingo is drawn across Hispaniola until the French colony of Saint-Domingue is established in the west.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: Santo Domingo (Spain)
features.source: Once Saint-Domingue is drawn in the west, Spanish Santo Domingo remains on the eastern part of Hispaniola until it is ceded to France at Basel.

features.label: Santo Domingo (Spain)
features.source: Retaken from France, then lost to Haiti. The two months of independent Spanish Haiti at the end are too brief to draw.

features.label: Santo Domingo (Spain)
features.source: Annexed at the Dominican president's invitation and abandoned after the War of Restoration.

features.name: Spanish Empire
features.label: Trinidad (Spain)
features.source: Claimed since Columbus but only durably settled with San José de Oruña in 1592; taken by a British expedition and kept at Amiens.
